blocks.text: 15. Using Tuning Systems
blocks.raw_html: 15. Using Tuning Systems

blocks.text: By default Live uses 12TET tuning, this means note pitches are divided equally into twelve parts per octave. However, there are numerous ways that pitches can be distributed across an octave or pseudo-octave (where notes are repeated at a different interval than an octave), and tuning systems can be used to specify these variations.
blocks.raw_html: By default Live uses 12TET tuning, this means note pitches are divided equally into twelve parts per octave. However, there are numerous ways that pitches can be distributed across an octave or pseudo-octave (where notes are repeated at a different interval than an octave), and tuning systems can be used to specify these variations.

blocks.text: Live 12 supports Scala files, which you can load into a Live Set to use a custom tuning for notes.
blocks.raw_html: Live 12 supports Scala files, which you can load into a Live Set to use a custom tuning for notes.

blocks.text: The Core Library also comes with a set of tuning systems, which can be found in the Tunings label of the browser. Tuning files from the Core Library use an Ableton-specific extension to the SCL (Scala) file format called ASCL.
blocks.raw_html: The Core Library also comes with a set of tuning systems, which can be found in the Tunings label of the browser. Tuning files from the Core Library use an Ableton-specific extension to the SCL (Scala) file format called ASCL.

blocks.text: When hovering over or selecting tuning systems in the browser, a short description of the tuning, including the number of notes per octave, is shown in the Info View. This description is also shown when hovering over the name of a loaded tuning system.
blocks.raw_html: When hovering over or selecting tuning systems in the browser, a short description of the tuning, including the number of notes per octave, is shown in the Info View. This description is also shown when hovering over the name of a loaded tuning system.

blocks.text: You can add your own .scl or .ascl files to any folder in Live’s Places so that they show up in the Tunings label of the browser under the User tag.
blocks.raw_html: You can add your own .scl or .ascl files to any folder in Live’s Places so that they show up in the Tunings label of the browser under the User tag.

blocks.text: All of Live’s built-in instruments are supported for use with tuning systems, as well as MPE-enabled plug-ins or external Max for Live instruments, provided that their pitch bend range is set to 48 semitones.
blocks.raw_html: All of Live’s built-in instruments are supported for use with tuning systems, as well as MPE-enabled plug-ins or external Max for Live instruments, provided that their pitch bend range is set to 48 semitones.

blocks.text: Note that instruments that are not MPE-enabled or use different pitch bend ranges are likely to play out of tune.

blocks.text: 15.1 Loading a Tuning System
blocks.raw_html: 15.1 Loading a Tuning System

blocks.text: To load a tuning system into a Set, you can double-click on a tuning file in the browser, or select the file and press Enter. These methods will automatically open the Tuning section of the browser, which is hidden by default.
blocks.raw_html: To load a tuning system into a Set, you can double-click on a tuning file in the browser, or select the file and press Enter. These methods will automatically open the Tuning section of the browser, which is hidden by default.

blocks.text: You can also open the Tuning section using the browser’s view control menu.
blocks.raw_html: You can also open the Tuning section using the browser’s view control menu.

blocks.text: External ASCL or SCL files on your computer can be dragged and dropped into the Tuning section as well. As long as the file is loaded in the Tuning section, the tuning will be saved with the Live Set.
blocks.raw_html: External ASCL or SCL files on your computer can be dragged and dropped into the Tuning section as well. As long as the file is loaded in the Tuning section, the tuning will be saved with the Live Set.

blocks.text: When a tuning system is added to a Live Set, the notes in the piano roll no longer represent standard MIDI notes, but instead show the corresponding notes of the tuning.
blocks.raw_html: When a tuning system is added to a Live Set, the notes in the piano roll no longer represent standard MIDI notes, but instead show the corresponding notes of the tuning.

blocks.text: You can hover over a note in the piano roll to see useful information, such as the note’s pitch and frequency, in the Status Bar. The specified pitch is produced when a note is played in the piano roll or via a keyboard.
blocks.raw_html: You can hover over a note in the piano roll to see useful information, such as the note’s pitch and frequency, in the Status Bar. The specified pitch is produced when a note is played in the piano roll or via a keyboard.

blocks.text: By default, if a tuning system is removed or changed to a different tuning, the position of existing notes in the piano roll is not changed, but the pitches shown in the note ruler are updated to match the new tuning. This means the original notes may not produce the same pitch.
blocks.raw_html: By default, if a tuning system is removed or changed to a different tuning, the position of existing notes in the piano roll is not changed, but the pitches shown in the note ruler are updated to match the new tuning. This means the original notes may not produce the same pitch.

blocks.text: The “Retune Set On Loading Tuning Systems” entry in the Options menu can be enabled so that when a tuning system is loaded or changed, the notes will closely match the pitches of the original notes, ensuring that a melody sounds as close to the original as possible. You will see a dialog appear to confirm this process when loading a tuning system.
blocks.raw_html: The “Retune Set On Loading Tuning Systems” entry in the Options menu can be enabled so that when a tuning system is loaded or changed, the notes will closely match the pitches of the original notes, ensuring that a melody sounds as close to the original as possible. You will see a dialog appear to confirm this process when loading a tuning system.

blocks.text: When automatic note retuning is enabled, removing or switching between tuning systems can cause original notes to be changed or lost. This can happen when two notes which overlap in time and originally had different pitches both get mapped to the same pitch in the new tuning system, as that new pitch is closest to both original pitches. In that case, one of the notes may be deleted or shortened.

blocks.text: Note that the Scale Mode choosers in Clip View and the Control Bar are no longer visible when a tuning system is loaded, and the devices that are scale aware have their Use Current Scale toggle disabled.

blocks.text: 15.2 The Tuning Section
blocks.raw_html: 15.2 The Tuning Section

blocks.text: Various pitch settings for a tuning system are accessible via the Tuning section.
blocks.raw_html: Various pitch settings for a tuning system are accessible via the Tuning section.

blocks.text: You can toggle the triangle next to the name of the tuning file to expand the section and access additional settings for the lowest and highest notes for the reference pitch.

blocks.text: Tuning displays the name of the tuning system.
blocks.raw_html: • Tuning displays the name of the tuning system.

blocks.text: Octave sets the octave of the note used for the reference pitch.
blocks.raw_html: • Octave sets the octave of the note used for the reference pitch.

blocks.text: Note sets the note in the octave used for the reference pitch.
blocks.raw_html: • Note sets the note in the octave used for the reference pitch.

blocks.text: Ref. Pitch/Freq sets the frequency of the reference pitch. The pitch of all notes in the Set can be raised or lowered by changing the frequency.
blocks.raw_html: • Ref. Pitch/Freq sets the frequency of the reference pitch. The pitch of all notes in the Set can be raised or lowered by changing the frequency.

blocks.text: Lowest Note sets what the lowest note plays by assigning it to an octave and pitch class. Changing the lowest note also affects the highest note, preserving the number of notes in between.
blocks.raw_html: • Lowest Note sets what the lowest note plays by assigning it to an octave and pitch class. Changing the lowest note also affects the highest note, preserving the number of notes in between.

blocks.text: Highest Note sets what the highest note plays; changing the highest note will also update the lowest note.

blocks.text: Note that the reference pitch is only audibly affected by the Ref. Pitch/Freq value. Changing the Octave or Note values will update the frequency displayed in the Ref. Pitch/Freq slider to match the newly specified notes, however, no audible change is produced until the reference pitch frequency value itself is adjusted. This is to prevent any sudden pitch changes when setting the Octave or Note values.

blocks.text: The floppy disk button to the right of the reference pitch frequency can be used to save the currently loaded tuning as an .ascl file to the Tunings label in the browser.

blocks.text: Pressing the arrow button next to the Save Tuning System button opens a link to Ableton’s Tuning website that contains more information about the loaded tuning system, as well as an interactive editor for trying out variations of the associated pitches. You can also export any custom tuning systems you create there. Note that not all tuning systems have external webpages, and the arrow button will be greyed out if no relevant link is available.

# Tuner device

This is the canonical partial contract for `SURF-DEVICE-TUNER` under
FEAT-DEVICES / FEAT-AUDIO in the [feature map](feature-map.md), following
[ADR 0005](../decisions/adr-0005-full-live-specification-coverage.md).
Inputs, controls, observable outputs and state are specified below; numerical
algorithms and unsupported lifecycle outcomes remain explicit gaps.

**D12 exact-target U:** D12 means the captured current official Version 12 manual,
not an observation of Live 12.4.3. Every D12 clause's exact-build applicability
is U. Dpkg means direct observation of retained files shipped in the target
package; it grades only stored bytes/values. No S or X audio/display claim is
made. U has no oracle and must never pass. All application cases are unexecuted.
This page is an analyst draft, not a released implementation input or complete
device specification. [Research and source limits](../research/device-audio-utilities.md)
own evidence synthesis; this page owns behavior.

The [device-chain/rack contract](device-racks.md) owns generic insertion,
reordering, activation, preset actions and deletion. [Set structure](live-set-structure.md)
and [ALS container](als-container.md) own their stated container/structure scopes;
their T1 device subset does not prove Tuner save/reopen. [Automation](automation-envelopes.md)
owns its envelope representation/evaluation clauses, not untraced device scheduling.
[Mix graph](mix-graph.md) owns track routing/mixing. [Mixer values](mixer-values.md)
describes track faders; it does not supply this device's gain, pan or smoothing law.
The current-manual source does not settle platform differences, keyboard access,
permissions, recovery, latency or transport coupling beyond explicit clauses.

## Requirements

### REQ-DEVICE-TUNER-001 — measurement input and transparent output

**D12.** Analyze incoming monophonic pitch and its distance from the nearest semitone. Tuner is a measurement device and does not alter the incoming audio. Clean monophonic signals are the intended input; polyphonic, noisy or harmonically rich inputs may give inaccurate results. No error or polyphonic-detection fallback is promised.

Evidence: `tuner:B02–B03`; [source locators](#analysis-only-evidence).

### REQ-DEVICE-TUNER-002 — view switching and tuning color

**D12.** The lower-left view buttons switch between Classic and Histogram views. Both use green for in tune and red for out of tune. Detection/green thresholds, hysteresis, intermediate colors and hold time are U.

Evidence: `tuner:B05`; [source locators](#analysis-only-evidence).

### REQ-DEVICE-TUNER-003 — Classic display

**D12.** Classic View shows a colored ball along a curve, the nearest detected note name in the center, and side arrows indicating whether tuning must move up or down. Exact note/octave spelling, pixels, ball displacement law and arrow thresholds are U.

Evidence: `tuner:B07`; [source locators](#analysis-only-evidence).

### REQ-DEVICE-TUNER-004 — Target Mode direction

**D12.** Target Mode has a central outline for desired pitch. The signal is in tune when the ball lies exactly within the outline; a sharp signal appears to its right, a flat signal to its left. This describes display semantics, not a quantified accepted cents band.

Evidence: `tuner:B08`; [source locators](#analysis-only-evidence).

### REQ-DEVICE-TUNER-005 — Strobe Mode

**D12.** Strobe Mode replaces the curve with a rotating light band. Rightward rotation means sharp; leftward means flat; a greater detuning makes the band move faster. Rotation speed, reference tolerance and freeze behavior are U.

Evidence: `tuner:B09`; [source locators](#analysis-only-evidence).

### REQ-DEVICE-TUNER-006 — Hertz and cents readout

**D12.** A switch selects incoming absolute frequency in Hz or distance from target in cents, and is visible in both Classic and Histogram views. Exact rounding, displayed precision, cents conversion, note-boundary tie handling and octave labeling are U.

Evidence: `tuner:B10, B14`; [source locators](#analysis-only-evidence).

### REQ-DEVICE-TUNER-007 — Histogram

**D12.** Histogram shows pitch over time and note names on its right scale. Horizontal gray lines indicate in-tune note centers; sharp notes lie above their lines and flat notes below. History length, vertical units, update cadence and handling of missing detections are U.

Evidence: `tuner:B12`; [source locators](#analysis-only-evidence).

### REQ-DEVICE-TUNER-008 — Histogram navigation and Auto

**D12.** Dragging vertically scrolls pitches; dragging horizontally zooms. Auto centers the display on incoming pitch. Auto/manual precedence, zoom limits and view-state retention are U.

Evidence: `tuner:B13`; [source locators](#analysis-only-evidence).

### REQ-DEVICE-TUNER-009 — note spelling menu

**D12.** Right-clicking anywhere within the view exposes three spelling choices: sharps, flats, or sharps and flats. Spelling changes labels; no pitch-processing change is documented. Exact key- or tuning-system-dependent enharmonic selection is U.

Evidence: `tuner:B16–B19`; [source locators](#analysis-only-evidence).

### REQ-DEVICE-TUNER-010 — reference pitch

**D12.** Reference changes the tuning reference used to analyze input; documented default is 440 Hz with an adjustable domain 410–480 Hz. Exact increment, text parsing, runtime default corroboration, reference convention under nonstandard tuning systems and output indication tolerances are U.

Evidence: `tuner:B21`; [source locators](#analysis-only-evidence).

### REQ-DEVICE-TUNER-011 — target persisted fields

**Dpkg.** The retained Tuner schema and Guitar Recording template show tuning frequency, view/readout/strobe state, histogram state, accidental spelling and IgnoreTuningSystem. The historical template stores TuningFreq/Manual=440. This is a saved example, not a 12.4.3 constructor/default or tuning-system behavioral contract.

Evidence: `PKG-SCHEMA:Tuner; package-values.json device=Tuner`; [source locators](#analysis-only-evidence).

### REQ-DEVICE-TUNER-012 — unresolved detection and lifecycle

**U.** Exact 12.4.3 applicability of every D12 clause remains U. Pitch algorithm, supported frequency/level/sample-rate range, confidence, silence/noise/polypitch fallback, latency, channel combination, transients, tuning-system interaction, persistence, automation, undo, cancellation, invalid files and teardown are unknown. No zero-cent or note-accuracy tolerance is invented.

Evidence: `No outcome evidence`; [source locators](#analysis-only-evidence).

L75: Why doesn't my .scl file produce the tuning I expect in Live?
L76: A .scl file defines a tuning system as a set of intervals, rather than determining the absolute frequencies of notes in the system. This means it defines the distance of each note in the system from some base pitch, which must be set via a “reference pitch” before note frequencies can be calculated. For example, in 12TET (twelve tone equal temperament tuning), the reference pitch A3 (the note A in the third octave) is typically defined with a frequency of 440Hz.
L77: Applying a different value, such as 432 Hz, results in different frequencies being calculated for all notes, even though the tuning system is still 12TET.
L78: A basic .scl file contains no reference pitch. In some cases, this can be supplied with a paired .kbm file. However, many software tools that import .scl files don’t support .kbm files. In this case, the software using the .scl file must apply a reference pitch, which can either be configurable via the tool’s UI or hardcoded. Live does not support .kbm files, but the .ascl files shipped with Live, unlike basic .scl files, do include a reference pitch.
L79: When a .scl file without a reference pitch is loaded, Live generates a reference pitch, in order to determine frequencies for all the notes in the tuning system, by assigning the frequency 440 Hz to a note near the middle of the 0-127 MIDI range. The remaining notes in the system are then derived from this reference. If you have a .scl file you’ve used previously in some other tool, it may sound different in Live, since that tool may have used a different strategy to determine the reference pitch.
L80: To correct this, you can try to determine the reference pitch used by that tool and adjust the reference pitch used in Live via the tuning UI. You can also do this “by ear”, and simply tweak the reference pitch in Live until it matches the tuning in the other tool.
L81: Once you’ve corrected the reference pitch, you can export your tuning from Live as a .ascl file so that you don’t need to repeat these steps every time you use that tuning in Live – the tuning will be exported as a .ascl file containing the custom reference pitch you set. Just click the Save icon in the tuning UI.
